steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using transformers for parameter estimation in statistics. Explain the parameter estimation problem and where MLE gets hard, describe our transformer-based approach and its advantages, and list the contributions and paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Parameter estimation and MLE (normal distribution example)
2. Harder cases: no closed form (Beta distribution)
3. Transformers for math tasks; our approach
4. Advantages over MLE and iterative methods
5. Contributions and paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Parameter estimation
- one of the most important tasks in statistics
- given distribution type + sample -> estimate parameters
- example: 1-dimensional normal, sample x_{1}, …, x_{N} from \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}); estimate \mu, \sigma
- most common: MLE (maximum likelihood estimation)
- \hat{\mu}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}}{N}, \hat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}{(x_{i}-\hat{\mu}})^{2}}{N}}; proof in a reference

2. Harder cases
- MLE for Beta distribution parameters has no closed form
- need numeric optimization: Newton-Raphson, gradient descent

3. Transformers + our approach
- transformers applied to many tasks incl. math: word problems, mathematical reasoning, symbolic regressions, time-series forecasting
- per distribution type: training set, each example = sample from distribution with predetermined parameters
- sample -> sequence of embeddings -> transformer predicts parameter(s)
- goal: as close as possible to true parameters, i.e. mean-square-error estimations

4. Advantages
- no mathematical derivation; complexity of pdf no burden, even without closed form MLE
- iterative methods (Newton-Raphson, gradient descent) used when no closed form
- vs iterative: single inference, not iterative; does not need the pdf at all
- bulb example: manufacturer tests percentage of two materials in filaments; bulb life distribution, single parameter = percentage of first material; unknown distribution, learn from bulb-life samples
- hyperparameter example: prediction error on random test case follows unknown distribution; estimate hyperparameters from error samples

5. Contributions + organization
- novel approach: transformers for parameter estimation
- sample -> sequence of embeddings, easily consumed, precise information
- comprehensive empirical study vs MLE for various distributions
- outperforms MLE on MSE for normal, exponential etc.; MLE still good (maximizes probability of sample); MSE one common way to evaluate
- Section 2 related work, Section 3 approach, Section 4 experiments, Section 5 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Parameter estimation is one of the most important tasks in statistics. If we know the type of the underlying distribution and have a sample of observations, a parameter estimation method should give an estimate of the parameters of the distribution. Take the 1-dimensional normal distribution as an example. Given a sample x_{1}, …, x_{N} drawn from normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), we want to estimate its parameters \mu and \sigma. The method that is used most often is MLE (maximum likelihood estimation). It is easy to prove that the MLE of \mu is \hat{\mu}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}}{N}, and the MLE of \sigma is \hat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}{(x_{i}-\hat{\mu}})^{2}}{N}}. The proof is in.

For some other distributions parameter estimation can be a lot more complex. For example, the maximum likelihood estimation of the parameters of a Beta distribution has been shown to have no closed form, so one has to use numeric optimization methods like the Newton-Raphson method or gradient descent to estimate the parameters.

In recent years transformer-based approaches have been applied successfully to many different tasks, and this includes many math tasks such as solving word problems, mathematical reasoning, symbolic regressions, and time-series forecasting. In this paper we propose a way to do parameter estimation with deep learning. For each type of distribution we generate a training set, and each training example has a sample drawn from a distribution with predetermined parameters. Then each sample is converted into a sequence of embeddings, and we train a transformer to predict the parameter(s) with the sequence as the input. We want the estimations to be as close as possible to the true parameters, so we are making mean-square-error estimations of the parameters.

4. Advantages
- no derivation needed; pdf complexity no burden even without closed-form MLE
- iterative methods (Newton-Raphson, gradient descent) used when no closed form
- ours: single inference, not iterative; doesn't need the pdf
- bulb example (two materials in filaments, life distribution, parameter = percentage of first material)
- hyperparameter example (prediction error distribution unknown)

5. Contributions
- transformers for parameter estimation
- sample -> sequence of embeddings
- empirical study vs MLE
- beats MLE on MSE for normal, exponential; MLE still good, MSE one common evaluation

6. Organization: Sections 2-5

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Parameter estimation is one of the most important tasks in statistics. If we know the type of the underlying distribution and have a sample of observations, a parameter estimation method should give an estimate of the parameters of the distribution. Take the 1-dimensional normal distribution as an example. Given a sample x_{1}, …, x_{N} drawn from normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), we want to estimate its parameters \mu and \sigma. The method that is used most often is MLE (maximum likelihood estimation). It is easy to prove that the MLE of \mu is \hat{\mu}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}}{N}, and the MLE of \sigma is \hat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}{(x_{i}-\hat{\mu}})^{2}}{N}}. The proof is in.

For some other distributions parameter estimation can be a lot more complex. For example, the maximum likelihood estimation of the parameters of a Beta distribution has been shown to have no closed form, so one has to use numeric optimization methods like the Newton-Raphson method or gradient descent to estimate the parameters.

In recent years transformer-based approaches have been applied successfully to many different tasks, and this includes many math tasks such as solving word problems, mathematical reasoning, symbolic regressions, and time-series forecasting. In this paper we propose a way to do parameter estimation with deep learning. For each type of distribution we generate a training set, and each training example has a sample drawn from a distribution with predetermined parameters. Then each sample is converted into a sequence of embeddings, and we train a transformer to predict the parameter(s) with the sequence as the input. We want the estimations to be as close as possible to the true parameters, so we are making mean-square-error estimations of the parameters.

The advantage of the approach is that it does not need any mathematical derivation. So the mathematical complexity of the probability density function is not a burden for the transformer model, even if there is no closed form solution to MLE for the parameters of the distribution. When there is no closed-form solution, iterative methods (such as Newton-Raphson method or gradient descent) have been used for estimating the parameters of a distribution. Our approach has two advantages compared to these methods. First, our approach is not iterative and only needs a single inference of a transformer model. Second, and this is more important, our approach does not even need to know the probability density function of the distribution. For example, say a manufacturer is testing the percentage of two materials in electrical filaments in bulbs. The life of a bulb follows a distribution with a single parameter, which is the percentage of the first material. Even if we don't know the distribution, we can still learn to estimate the parameter from many samples of bulb lives. Another example is testing the hyperparameters of a particular deep learning model, where the prediction error on a random test case follows a distribution we don't know. But we can still estimate the hyperparameters from samples of such errors.

Overall, the contributions of this paper are:

- • We present a novel approach that uses transformers for parameter estimation.

- • We propose a way to convert a sample of a distribution into a sequence of embeddings, which a transformer can easily consume and which can carry precise information about the sample.

- • We do a comprehensive empirical study that compares our approach with maximum likelihood estimation methods for various distributions.

- • We show that our approach outperforms MLE when measured by mean-square-error (MSE) in most commonly used distributions like normal distribution and exponential distribution. This does not mean MLE is not a good method, since it always maximizes the probability of observing a sample. Our experiment just shows that our method beats MLE in terms of mean-square-error in most scenarios, and that is one common way to evaluate a method of parameter estimation.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 presents related work. Section 3 describes our approach for parameter estimation with a transformer. Section 4 reports experimental results and Section 5 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Parameter estimation is one of the most important tasks in statistics. Given the type of the underlying distribution and a sample of observations, a parameter estimation method should produce an estimate of the distribution’s parameters. Take the 1-dimensional normal distribution as an example. Given a sample x_{1}, …, x_{N} drawn from normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), we hope to estimate its parameters \mu and \sigma. The most commonly used method is MLE (maximum likelihood estimation). It can be easily proven that the MLE of \mu is \hat{\mu}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}}{N}, and that of \sigma is \hat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}{(x_{i}-\hat{\mu}})^{2}}{N}}. The proof can be found in [1].

Parameter estimation for some other distributions can be much more complex. For example, it has been shown that the maximum likelihood estimation for the parameters of a Beta distribution has no closed form [2], so one needs to resort to numeric optimization methods such as the Newton-Raphson method or gradient descent to estimate its parameters.

In recent years transformer-based approaches have been successfully applied to many diverse tasks, including many math tasks such as solving word problems [3], mathematical reasoning [4], symbolic regressions [5], and time-series forecasting [6]. In this paper we propose an approach to perform parameter estimation using deep learning. For each type of distribution, we generate a training set in which each training example contains a sample drawn from a distribution with predetermined parameters. We then convert each sample into a sequence of embeddings and train a transformer to predict the parameter(s) with the sequence as the input. We aim at producing estimations that are as close as possible to the true parameters, i.e., we are making mean-square-error estimations of the parameters.

The advantage of our approach is that it does not require any mathematical derivation. Thus the mathematical complexity of the probability density function does not pose any burden for the transformer model, even when there is no closed form solution to MLE for the parameters of the distribution. Iterative methods (such as the Newton-Raphson method or gradient descent) have been used for estimating the parameters of a distribution when there is no closed-form solution (e.g., [7]). Compared to such methods, our approach has two advantages. Firstly, it is not iterative and requires just a single inference of a transformer model. Secondly, and more importantly, it does not even require knowing the probability density function of the distribution. For example, suppose a manufacturer is testing the percentage of two materials in electrical filaments in bulbs. The life of a bulb follows a distribution with a single parameter, which is the percentage of the first material. Even if the distribution is unknown to us, we can still learn to estimate the parameter from many samples of bulb lives. As another example, when testing the hyperparameters of a particular deep learning model, the prediction error on a random test case follows a distribution that is unknown to us, but we can estimate the hyperparameters based on samples of such errors.

In general, we make the following contributions in this paper:

- • We present a novel approach to use transformers for parameter estimation.

- • We propose a way to convert a sample of a distribution into a sequence of embeddings, which can be easily consumed by a transformer and can carry precise information about the sample.

- • We conduct a comprehensive empirical study comparing our approach with maximum likelihood estimation methods for various distributions.

- • We show that, when measured by mean-square-error (MSE), our approach outperforms MLE in most commonly used distributions such as normal distribution and exponential distribution. Note that this does not indicate MLE is not a good method, as it always maximizes the probability of observing a sample. Our experiment simply indicates that our method beats MLE in terms of mean-square-error in most scenarios, which is one common way to evaluate a method of parameter estimation.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents related work. Section 3 describes our approach for parameter estimation with a transformer. Experimental results are reported in Section 4, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

References:
[1] Meyer, J.: Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Gaussian Parameters. In: http://jrmeyer.github.io/machinelearning/2017/08/18/mle.html. Accessed Oct 4, 2023.
[2] Owen, C.-E.: Parameter Estimation for the Beta Distribution. M.S. diss. Dept. of Statistics, Brigham Young University. (2008)
[3] Cobbe, K. et al.: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems. https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168. (2021)
[4] Lu, P. et al.: A Survey of Deep Learning for Mathematical Reasoning. In: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pp. 14605-14631. Association for Computer Linguistics, Toronto, Canada. (2023)
[5] Cranmer, M. et al.: Discovering Symbolic Models from Deep Learning with Inductive Biases. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11287. (2020)
[6] Lim, B., Zohren, S.: Time Series Forecasting With Deep Learning: A Survey. https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.13408. (2020)
[7] Gnanadesikan, R. et al.: Maximum Likelihood Estimation of the Parameters of the Beta Distribution from Smallest Order Statistics. In: Technometrics, 9 (4), pp. 607-620. (1967)
